h1: Oil Tank Removal in St. John's and the Avalon Peninsula
heroSub: Once a tank is disconnected, the province gives you 30 days to get it out (10 if it leaked). We drain it, cut it down, haul it away and leave the site clean, with outdoor removals at a flat $500.
introHtml:
Oil tank removal in St. John's isn't something you can put off. Under NLR 60/03, the Heating Oil Storage Tank System Regulations, a disconnected tank has to be emptied, dismantled and disposed of within 30 days, and within 10 days if it leaked or took on water. Harbour Tank Co does the whole job: we pump out the leftover oil, clean out the sludge, take the tank apart, cap the lines and take everything away.

Most people call us for one of three reasons. The tag expired and the delivery driver wouldn't fill, they've switched to electric heat and the old tank is still sitting there, or a leak forced the issue. Whatever brought you here, you'll get a free written estimate, a flat $500 price on outdoor tanks, and a crew that knows the rules. Call (709) 800-3117, or keep reading for what's involved.

sections.heading: What's included in an oil tank removal
sections.html:
The regulation spells out what a proper removal looks like, and we follow it step by step. Here's what happens when our crew arrives at your home in St. John's, Mount Pearl, Paradise, Portugal Cove-St. Philip's or anywhere on the Northeast Avalon.

  • Pump out the oil. Whatever's left in the tank is pumped into sealed drums. If you're getting a new tank the same day, clean oil can usually go straight into it.
  • Remove the sludge. Years of water and sediment settle at the bottom. That gets scraped out and drummed separately.
  • Disconnect and dismantle. The supply line and filter come off, then the tank is cut down or lifted out whole, depending on where it sits.
  • Cap or remove the piping. Fill and vent lines are pulled or capped at the wall so a driver can't fill a tank that's gone.
  • Dispose of everything. Steel goes for scrap, fibreglass goes to a facility that accepts it, and oil and sludge go to a waste-oil handler.
  • Restore the site. Stand and pad are removed, the ground is levelled or the floor swept, and the spot is left ready for whatever comes next.

If the tank is being replaced, our oil tank replacement price already includes taking the old one away. This page is for stand-alone removals where nothing is going back in.

sections.heading: The 30-day rule, and the 10-day rule after a leak
sections.html:
Section 16(3) of NLR 60/03 says that within 30 days of disconnecting a tank, the owner has to empty it, remove the sludge and residual oil, dismantle and dispose of it, remove or cap the piping and restore the site. Section 18(5) shortens that to 10 days if the tank leaked or took on water, with another 30 days allowed for cleaning up the ground. These aren't suggestions. They're the law, and they apply to every homeowner on the Avalon.

Where most people run into this is the HOST tag. Every registered tank carries a metal tag with a six-digit number and an expiry stamped in month-year form, so "7-2028" means the tank can't be used after 31 July 2028. Once that date passes, the driver isn't allowed to deliver under section 13(1)(b)(ii), and they're required to report it. That's the refused-delivery phone call nobody wants in February.

If your tag has already expired, start with our expired oil tank emergency page. If you're not sure whether to remove and replace or just remove, call (709) 800-3117 and we'll talk it through. There's no charge for the estimate either way.

sections.heading: Oil tank removal cost in St. John's
sections.html:
Removal and disposal of an outdoor domestic tank is $500 CAD. That covers the pump-out, sludge removal, dismantling, capping the lines, hauling and disposal. It's the same price in Torbay, Conception Bay South or Bay Roberts as it is in the city.

Indoor and basement tanks are quoted case by case. There's no honest way to put one number on them, because the price depends on things we have to see: how many stairs, how wide the doorway, whether the tank has to be cut in place, and how much sludge is in the bottom. We'll give you a written figure before anyone picks up a tool.

A few things worth knowing. If you're replacing the tank, don't pay for removal twice. Our replacement pricing already includes taking the old tank away. And if a leak is involved, the removal price doesn't cover soil remediation, which is a separate job with its own 30-day window under the regulation.

sections.heading: Switching to electric? The old tank still has to go
sections.html:
A lot of removal jobs on the Avalon right now come from oil-to-electric conversions. The federal Oil to Heat Pump Affordability grant closed to new applications on 31 July 2026, and the takeCHARGE Oil to Electric general stream closed on 31 March 2026, so the big rebates are gone for most households. The low- and moderate-income takeCHARGE stream runs to 31 March 2027 if you qualify. Either way, the removal rule doesn't change: once the tank is disconnected, the 30-day clock starts.

Some homeowners figure they'll leave the old tank in place and deal with it later. The trouble is that "later" tends to arrive when the house is being sold. Confirmation of a tank's registration is often asked for by an insurance company, or by a lawyer or realtor when a home changes hands, and an old tank nobody can account for is a question you don't want on closing day. Getting it done now, while the heat pump crew is already on site, is simpler than scrambling before a closing date.

As for what happens to the tank itself: the steel is cut into sections and sent for scrap recycling. Fibreglass tanks can't be scrapped, so they go to a facility that accepts them. The oil, water and sludge are drummed and sent to a waste-oil handler, never poured out on the ground.

If you'd rather keep oil as backup heat alongside the heat pump, a 100-gallon steel tank installed is $3,100 and the old tank's removal is included in that price. And if you're staying on oil for good, our fibreglass tank upgrade page explains why some Avalon tanks now carry tags stamped decades out instead of years.

faq.q: How much does oil tank removal cost in St. John's?
faq.a: Removal and disposal of an outdoor domestic tank is $500 CAD, including the pump-out, sludge removal, dismantling, capping the lines and hauling. Indoor and basement tanks are quoted case by case after we see the access. Every estimate is free and in writing. Call (709) 800-3117 to book one.

faq.q: How long do I have to remove a disconnected oil tank in Newfoundland?
faq.a: Under section 16(3) of NLR 60/03, you have 30 days from the date the tank is disconnected to empty it, remove it, cap the piping and restore the site. If the tank leaked or took on water, section 18(5) cuts that to 10 days, with 30 more days allowed for cleaning up any contaminated ground. Book the removal as soon as the tank comes offline so you're not racing the calendar.

faq.q: I'm switching to a heat pump. Do I still have to remove the oil tank?
faq.a: Yes. Disconnecting the tank starts the 30-day removal clock whether or not a new heating system is going in. The federal Oil to Heat Pump Affordability grant closed to new applications on 31 July 2026 and the takeCHARGE general stream closed on 31 March 2026, so don't count on rebate money to cover the removal. The low- and moderate-income takeCHARGE stream continues to 31 March 2027 if you qualify for it.

faq.q: What happens to the old tank and the oil inside it?
faq.a: We pump the remaining oil into sealed drums, then scrape out the sludge and water from the bottom and drum that separately. If you're getting a new tank the same day, clean oil can usually be transferred into it rather than thrown away. The steel is cut down and sent for scrap recycling, fibreglass tanks go to a facility that accepts them, and the oil and sludge go to a waste-oil handler. Nothing is left on your property.

faq.q: My tank is leaking. What do I do first?
faq.a: Call (709) 800-3117 right away; the emergency line is answered 24/7. Shut the supply valve at the tank if you can reach it safely, keep people and pets away from the spot, and don't try to move the tank yourself. Under section 18(5) you have 10 days to get the tank removed once a leak is found, so the sooner we're on site, the more options you have. After-hours pricing varies by contractor and by job, so ask when you call and you'll get a figure before anyone starts.
